analysis.one_liner: Regulates private equity and for-profit ownership of hospitals and clinics, with public disclosure and licensing.
analysis.headline: The Health Over Wealth Act, introduced by Sen. Markey and 7 Senate colleagues, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no further action since July 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force for-profit companies and private equity funds that own hospitals, nursing homes, hospices, doctor practices, and other health care providers to publicly disclose their finances: debt levels, fees they extract, dividends, facility closures, staffing ratios, wage cuts, labor violations, and political spending. It would require private equity funds to get a federal license before buying a health care provider, let the Health Secretary deny or revoke those licenses for price gouging, understaffing, or access barriers, and let the Secretary temporarily block private equity health care takeovers while a new task force studies them. It would also require hospitals to give 90 days' notice before closing or cutting essential services, submit a mitigation plan, and face a public comment process, and it would strip favorable tax treatment from real estate investment trusts that own health care property.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and communities served by hospitals, nursing homes, and clinics owned by private equity or other for-profit firms, who would learn who owns their providers, what debt and fees sit on them, and when a facility plans to close or cut services. Health care workers benefit from required disclosure of staffing ratios, wage cuts, and labor law complaints, and pension participants benefit from a bankruptcy rule putting pension withdrawal liabilities first in line for payment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health workers, and pension holders

how_it_helps.text: Requires for-profit health care owners, and especially private equity-controlled firms, to publicly report debt, fund fees, dividends extracted, asset sales, facility closures, staffing levels, wage reductions, and labor law complaints, with government audits to verify the data [S2].

Requires private equity funds to obtain a federal license to invest in health care entities, which the Secretary can deny or revoke for price gouging, understaffing, or access barriers, with revoked firms forced to divest [S2].

Lets the Secretary require private equity-controlled firms to set aside escrow funding covering at least 5 years of operating costs to protect communities if a provider closes or cuts essential services, and lets the Secretary block private equity health care purchases until a new task force finishes studying abuses in specific sectors [S2].

Requires hospitals to notify the government 90 days before closing or discontinuing essential services, submit a public mitigation plan, go through a public comment period, and face potential Medicare enrollment bans for violating the rules [S2].

Amends federal bankruptcy law to put multiemployer pension withdrawal liability first among payment priorities when a health care business goes bankrupt, and directs bankruptcy courts to weigh regional health care access when confirming health care reorganization plans [S2].

Removes the favorable tax treatment of rents from health care property for real estate investment trusts and bars sale-leaseback deals whose terms would weaken a health care entity's finances or put public health at risk [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, health care real estate investment trusts, and for-profit hospital and nursing home operators bear new reporting, licensing, escrow, and penalty costs, and lose favorable tax treatment on health care real estate. Compliance costs could ultimately be passed to patients or used as a reason to exit marginal facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and for-profit health care owners

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes an extensive annual reporting regime on all for-profit firms owning health care providers, not just private equity ones, and although it directs the Secretary to reduce administrative burden, the compliance costs are real and could fall on small operators or be passed into health care prices [S2].

The licensing, escrow, and moratorium powers give the Health Secretary wide discretion to block or unwind health care investments; investors and some health economists argue this could dry up the capital that distressed rural and community hospitals rely on, potentially accelerating closures the bill is trying to prevent [S2].

The escrow requirement to cover at least 5 years of operating and capital expenditures is a high financial bar that could keep for-profit buyers out of struggling facilities altogether, with no guaranteed nonprofit or public buyer waiting to replace them [S2].

Many of the bill's central tools are studies, reports, and a task force; the research mandate explicitly contemplates a future transition to an outright ban on for-profit ownership rather than enacting one, so the bill's practical limits on private equity depend heavily on future rulemaking by whichever administration holds the Secretary's office [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core value for ordinary people is visibility and leverage: public disclosure of who owns their hospital and what has been extracted from it, advance notice before closures, and a license with teeth for the private equity buyers most linked in research to understaffing and hospital distress. Those gains are real but mostly preventive and depend on aggressive enforcement by the Secretary. The costs fall on the regulated industries and, potentially, on patients through compliance costs or lost access to investment capital for struggling facilities. It is a regulatory-transparency bill with strong guardrails for closures, not an outright ban, which limits both its benefits and its downside.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no markup, no hearing, and no floor action so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the Health Over Wealth Act on July 23, 2026, joined by Sens. Sanders, Warren, Blumenthal, Merkley, Baldwin, Booker, and Smith as original cosponsors [S2].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in its history [S4].
The cosponsor list totals 7 senators: 6 of 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents, with no Republican support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds, health care REITs, and for-profit health care owners are better off so far, because the bill has made no progress beyond committee referral in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 seats and none have supported it. Communities facing private equity-owned hospital and nursing home closures remain without the disclosure and closure protections the bill would create.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and for-profit health owners, so far

industries.industry: Private equity funds investing in health care
industries.note: The bill requires PE funds to be licensed before buying health care providers, exposes their fees, debt loads, dividends, and political spending to public disclosure, allows revocation of licenses and divestment for understaffing or price gouging, and permits a purchase moratorium while a task force studies abuses. Research linking PE ownership of nursing homes and hospitals to worse staffing and outcomes is the basis for the bill.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill strips REIT tax advantages on rents from health care property and requires federal review of hospital sale-leaseback deals that would weaken a facility's finances. These arrangements are how many hospital sale-leasebacks load operators with rising rent obligations.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital and nursing home operators
industries.note: All for-profit owners face annual public reporting on debt, executive pay, staffing, wage cuts, closures, and labor violations, plus 90-day closure notices and mitigation plans for hospitals. Compliant operators gain a level disclosure playing field, but the escrow, license, and penalty regimes raise their costs.

industries.industry: Financial institutions lending to health care buyouts
industries.note: The bill requires disclosure of who holds the debt on PE-owned health firms, including foreign creditors, and the bankruptcy change that puts pension withdrawal liability first makes lending to heavily leveraged health care buyouts riskier.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no action since referral, no Republican support, and a Senate majority of 55 Republicans controlling the committee and floor agenda. Bills introduced this late in a Congress with one-sided sponsorship and no committee action almost never reach a vote, so the most likely path is that it dies in committee when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless supporters fold pieces of it into a larger health care package.
